requirements.requirement: node2 is segmented onto its own VLAN 10 over the shared link
requirements.summary: node2's eth1 was configured with an 802.1Q sub-interface eth1.10 (10.10.10.2/24), persisted in /etc/network/interfaces and brought up via ifupdown-ng. tcpdump on node1's physical eth1 directly confirms outbound frames from node2's MAC are tagged 'vlan 10' (802.1Q ethertype 0x8100), proving genuine VLAN segmentation rather than coincidental L3 routing.

requirements.requirement: node3 is segmented onto its own VLAN 20 over the shared link
requirements.summary: node3's eth1 was configured with sub-interface eth1.20 (10.10.20.2/24), persisted and brought up. tcpdump confirms node3's frames are tagged 'vlan 20' on the shared physical link.

requirements.requirement: node1 routes between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20
requirements.summary: VyOS node1 configured with eth1 vif 10 (10.10.10.1/24) and vif 20 (10.10.20.1/24) sub-interfaces, committed and saved; ip_forward=1 confirmed enabled, and node1's eth1 shows both VLAN-tagged ICMP request/reply traffic passing through it during the cross-VLAN ping, directly showing it acting as the routing point between the two VLANs.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 can still reach each other despite being placed on separate VLANs
requirements.summary: Bidirectional ping between 10.10.10.2 (node2) and 10.10.20.2 (node3) succeeds with 0% loss and ttl=63 (one less than a directly-connected ttl=64 would show), directly confirming a routed hop through node1 rather than a flat bridged link.

requirements.requirement: VLAN/routing configuration survives a reboot on each node (supporting durability of the segmentation, implied by making config persistent)
requirements.summary: For all three nodes, a pre-restart boot_id was captured, a native reboot was issued and acknowledged, connectivity was lost during the transition (repeated connection errors), a new distinct post-restart boot_id was observed, and after recovery the VLAN interfaces/addresses/routes and IP forwarding were confirmed present and re-verified end-to-end (pings between node2 and node3 succeeded again after each of the three reboots, including node1's own reboot).

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were directly and coherently demonstrated: node2 is genuinely 802.1Q-tagged onto VLAN 10 and node3 onto VLAN 20 over the shared eth1 link (confirmed by a live tcpdump capture showing tag 10 and tag 20 frames, not just IP addressing), node1 is configured and observed acting as the router between the two VLANs (ip_forward enabled, VLAN sub-interfaces addressed, and both VLANs' traffic transiting node1's shared interface during the test), and node2/node3 successfully ping each other with a ttl decrement consistent with a routed (not bridged) path. Configuration was made persistent on all nodes, and the separately-required provider-wide restart evidence protocol was executed and captured for all three nodes with pre-restart boot IDs, reboot acknowledgements, distinct post-restart boot IDs, and confirmed recovery of VLAN configuration, forwarding, and end-to-end connectivity after each reboot.
limitations: The bounded evidence trace does not show a complete `show configuration commands` VyOS dump confirming persisted vif config after `save`, only ip/sysctl state checks and a post-reboot verification that inferred persistence; this is adequate but slightly indirect for the persistence claim specifically (separate from the boot-id-based restart recovery, which is directly observed).

tcpdump verification of VLAN tagging was only performed on node1's physical eth1 during the node2-to-node3 direction; there is no separate raw-frame capture directly on node2 or node3's physical NIC, though this is a reasonable and sufficient vantage point since it is the shared link itself.

operational_hygiene.summary: One bounded, low-risk troubleshooting mutation was identified: on node2, the executor created a test VLAN interface eth1.10 (cmd-b3baa742dce44782) before settling on the persistent /etc/network/interfaces-based configuration, and then deleted it again (cmd-f157b3772272412a) before applying the final config. This left no residue and was fully reverted. All other state-changing commands (VyOS configure/commit/save, Alpine /etc/network/interfaces edits and ifup, module probes, tcpdump captures, and the three reboots) map directly to satisfying the VLAN/routing requirement, verifying it, or executing the separately-required restart evidence protocol. The lifecycle diff between after-prepare and after-executor shows only expected reboot-induced changes (new boot IDs, new PIDs in listening-socket output, new systemd temp dirs, and a small /tmp/reboot.log artifact per Alpine node from the reboot scheduling command) — none of these represent unwanted residue, damaged package state, or weakened security posture. Package-health checks (apk/dpkg) show no new inconsistencies pre- vs post-executor.
